title: Context API Deep Dive — Performance, Splitting, and Patterns

subChunks.title: Context API Deep Dive — Performance, Splitting, and Patterns
subChunks.hookHtml: You've used Context to avoid prop drilling. At Senior level, the question is more nuanced: when is Context the right abstraction, when does it hurt performance, and how do you structure contexts so they scale? This lesson covers context performance characteristics, the context-splitting pattern, and the canonical provider + custom hook pattern used in production codebases.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Creating and providing context

import { createContext, useContext, useState } from 'react';

// 1. Create the context with a default value:
const ThemeContext = createContext('light');

// 2. Provide it from a parent — all descendants can access it:
function App() {
  const [theme, setTheme] = useState('light');
  return (
    <ThemeContext.Provider value={{ theme, setTheme }}>
      <PageLayout />
    </ThemeContext.Provider>
  );
}

// 3. Consume it in any descendant — no props needed:
function ThemeToggle() {
  const { theme, setTheme } = useContext(ThemeContext);
  return (
    <button onClick={() => setTheme(t => t === 'light' ? 'dark' : 'light')}>
      Current: {theme}
    </button>
  );
}

The canonical pattern — Provider + custom hook

Wrapping useContext in a custom hook gives better error messages and a cleaner import API:

export const ThemeContext = createContext(null);

export function ThemeProvider({ children }) {
  const [theme, setTheme] = useState('light');
  return (
    <ThemeContext.Provider value={{ theme, setTheme }}>
      {children}
    </ThemeContext.Provider>
  );
}

export function useTheme() {
  const context = useContext(ThemeContext);
  if (!context) {
    throw new Error('useTheme must be used within a ThemeProvider');
  }
  return context;
}

// In any component — clean and safe:
const { theme, setTheme } = useTheme();

Context performance — the re-render problem

Vex: "Context is not a state management system. It's a dependency injection system. The most common Context misuse I see: using it for state that changes frequently (like a list of items a user is editing). Every consumer re-renders when the context value changes. For high-frequency state, use a dedicated state manager or keep state local."

Good uses for Context: authentication state, theme, locale, feature flags, app-wide config that rarely changes.

Poor uses for Context: lists that mutate frequently, form state, real-time counters.

Performance: splitting contexts

If your context value changes frequently, split it. Consumers of the stable parts won't re-render when only the dynamic part changes:

// ❌ One context — every request re-renders all consumers:
<AuthContext.Provider value={{ user, loading, refetch }}>

// ✅ Two contexts — stable consumers never re-render on loading changes:
<AuthUserContext.Provider value={user}>
  <AuthActionsContext.Provider value={{ loading, refetch }}>
    {children}
  </AuthActionsContext.Provider>
</AuthUserContext.Provider>

Stabilising the context value with useMemo

// ❌ New object on every Provider re-render — all consumers re-render:
<ThemeContext.Provider value={{ theme, setTheme }}>

// ✅ Stable reference — consumers only re-render when theme changes:
const value = useMemo(() => ({ theme, setTheme }), [theme]);
<ThemeContext.Provider value={value}>

storyBeats.text: Grand Archmage Solomon appears at Vex's workshop. He holds up a tangled web of scroll-ropes — props passed through a dozen components.

storyBeats.speaker: Grand Archmage Solomon
storyBeats.text: The authenticated wizard's identity. The academy's chosen theme. The active tongue. These values do not belong to one component — they belong to the entire system. Passing them through every doorway is not architecture. It is chaos.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: Context solves prop drilling for values many components need. But every consumer re-renders when the context value changes. Wrap it in a custom hook for safety. Split contexts to isolate fast-changing state from slow-changing state. Memoize the value object so the reference stays stable.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build a theme system using Context:

  • Create a ThemeContext with createContext
  • Build a <ThemeProvider children /> that owns a theme state ('light' or 'dark') and provides { theme, toggleTheme }. Memoize the value object with useMemo.
  • Build a useTheme() custom hook that reads from ThemeContext and throws if used outside the provider
  • Build a <ThemeToggle /> component that uses useTheme() to display the current theme and toggle it

guidedPracticeTests.label: Clicking again changes back to light

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build an AuthContext system from scratch. It should provide { user, login, logout }. user is null when logged out, or { name: string } when logged in. login(name) sets the user; logout() clears it. Build a <UserGreeting> component that shows either 'Welcome, {name}' or a Login button. Split the context into AuthUserContext (stable) and AuthActionsContext (actions). Demonstrate that a component consuming only user doesn't re-render when only actions change.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain React Context to a colleague who only knows prop drilling. Walk through the three steps. Then explain the main performance caveat — what re-renders when context changes, and how context splitting and value memoization address it.

questions.prompt: When a Context value changes, which components re-render?
options: All components that call useContext() with that specific context
All components in the entire application
Only the Provider component and its direct children
Only components that are currently visible on screen
questions.answer: All components that call useContext() with that specific context
questions.explanation: React re-renders every component that subscribed to a context (via useContext) when that context's value changes. Components in between that don't call useContext are not re-rendered. This is why putting frequently-changing state in context can cause performance problems — many consumers may re-render unnecessarily.

questions.prompt: What does `createContext(null)` return and what is the `null` argument?
options: A Context object; null is the default value used when a component consumes the context without a Provider above it
A Context object; null disables the context so it can only be used when a Provider is present
A Provider component; null sets the initial state to empty
A hook factory; null means the context will not trigger re-renders
questions.answer: A Context object; null is the default value used when a component consumes the context without a Provider above it
questions.explanation: The argument to createContext is the default value — returned by useContext when there is no matching Provider above the consumer in the tree. null is a common choice for contexts that require a Provider (your custom hook can then throw a helpful error). A meaningful default (like 'light' for a theme) lets components work without a Provider in tests or Storybook.

questions.prompt: Why do most production codebases wrap `useContext` in a custom hook instead of calling it directly?
options: To throw a clear error when the hook is used outside its Provider, and to give consumers a cleaner import API
Because useContext cannot be called directly — it requires a wrapper
To improve performance by memoizing the context value automatically
To avoid importing the Context object in every consumer file
questions.answer: To throw a clear error when the hook is used outside its Provider, and to give consumers a cleaner import API
questions.explanation: Without the wrapper, using useContext outside a Provider silently returns the default value (often null), causing confusing null reference errors. The wrapper throws a descriptive error immediately. As a bonus, consumers import useTheme() rather than both useContext and ThemeContext — one import, not two.

questions.prompt: An AuthContext provides `{ user, isLoading, refetch }`. Many components only need `user`, but `isLoading` changes on every request. What is the performance implication and the fix?
options: All useContext(AuthContext) consumers re-render on every request. Fix: split into UserContext (stable) and AuthStatusContext (dynamic) — most components only subscribe to UserContext
There is no issue — React only re-renders components that use the changed value
Memoize the context value with useMemo to prevent unnecessary re-renders
Move refetch outside the context to prevent isLoading changes from propagating
questions.answer: All useContext(AuthContext) consumers re-render on every request. Fix: split into UserContext (stable) and AuthStatusContext (dynamic) — most components only subscribe to UserContext
questions.explanation: Context doesn't do value-level change detection — any change to the Provider's value prop triggers a re-render in all consumers. Since isLoading toggles true/false on every request, every useContext(AuthContext) component re-renders twice per request. Splitting contexts means components needing only the user object subscribe to UserContext and are never re-rendered by loading state changes.
